sections.s6_takeaway:
A liveness probe and a readiness probe answer two different questions, and the whole art is keeping them separate. The liveness probe asks "is this process healthy, or is it wedged and should be restarted?" If it fails the configured number of times, Kubernetes kills and recreates the container. The readiness probe asks "is this Pod able to serve traffic right now?" If it fails, Kubernetes removes the Pod from the Service's load-balancing pool but leaves it running so it can recover and rejoin. Restarting is the response to liveness failure; pausing traffic is the response to readiness failure.

The most important rule is what each probe may check. The liveness probe must check only the process's own internal state and must never check external dependencies like the database. If liveness checked the database and the database had a brief hiccup, every Pod would fail liveness at the same instant and Kubernetes would restart the entire fleet, turning a two-second blip into a full outage. The readiness probe, on the other hand, may check dependencies, because the correct response to a missing dependency is to stop taking traffic, not to restart.

In Spring Boot I wire this with Actuator's health groups and application availability. I enable the probes so Actuator publishes two grouped endpoints: the liveness group includes only the internal liveness state, and the readiness group includes the readiness state plus dependency and warm-up indicators. On the Kubernetes side, the liveness probe does an HTTP GET on the liveness path and the readiness probe on the readiness path, and I use a startup probe to cover the JVM's slow boot so liveness never kills a container that is merely still starting. Spring Boot also manages these states automatically during graceful shutdown: it flips readiness to refusing-traffic first so the load balancer drains the Pod before the process exits.

At National Bank of India this separation is what made our deploys invisible to customers. When a new Transfer Service Pod started, it reported not-ready until its connection pool was filled and its currency-rate cache was primed, so Kubernetes only routed customers to it once it could truly serve them. When the database had an occasional blip, readiness dropped and the Pod was pulled from the pool for a moment, but liveness stayed up so nothing was restarted, and the Pod rejoined the instant the database recovered. And during rolling updates, old Pods drained gracefully so in-flight transfers completed. Accurate probes were not a nicety; they were the exact mechanism that turned the objective of zero-downtime deployment into reality.

---

answers.question: How is Kibana configured in your project, and how does the ELK stack enable centralized logging and request tracing with correlation IDs?
answers.shortTitle: Kibana configuration and how the ELK stack enables centralized logging and request tracing with correlation IDs

s1_definition.profdef: The ELK stack is three tools working together: Elasticsearch stores and indexes logs for fast search, Logstash or the lighter Beats agents collect and parse logs from every service and ship them to Elasticsearch, and Kibana is the web interface for searching, visualising, and dashboarding those logs. Centralized logging means every microservice writes structured JSON logs that are shipped into one searchable Elasticsearch cluster instead of sitting in files on scattered Pods. Request tracing with correlation IDs means each incoming request is assigned a unique identifier that is attached to every log line produced while handling it and propagated to downstream services, so in Kibana you can filter by that one ID and see the complete journey of a single request across every service it touched.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India has fifty branches, each keeping its own paper logbook. When a customer complains "my transfer failed," staff would have to phone every branch and flip through separate books. ELK is like scanning every branch's logbook into one central searchable computer. The correlation ID is like stamping a single reference number on every form a customer's request touches as it moves from the teller to the back office to the vault — so later you type that one number into Kibana and instantly see every step the request took, in order, no matter which department handled it.
s1_definition.oneliner: ELK pools every service's logs into one searchable place, and a correlation ID lets you pull the complete story of a single request out of billions of log lines with one filter.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The ELK stack is three tools working together: Elasticsearch stores and indexes logs for fast search, Logstash or the lighter Beats agents collect and parse logs from every service and ship them to Elasticsearch, and Kibana is the web interface for searching, visualising, and dashboarding those logs. Centralized logging means every microservice writes structured JSON logs that are shipped into one searchable Elasticsearch cluster instead of sitting in files on scattered Pods. Request tracing with correlation IDs means each incoming request is assigned a unique identifier that is attached to every log line produced while handling it and propagated to downstream services, so in Kibana you can filter by that one ID and see the complete journey of a single request across every service it touched.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India has fifty branches, each keeping its own paper logbook. When a customer complains "my transfer failed," staff would have to phone every branch and flip through separate books. ELK is like scanning every branch's logbook into one central searchable computer. The correlation ID is like stamping a single reference number on every form a customer's request touches as it moves from the teller to the back office to the vault — so later you type that one number into Kibana and instantly see every step the request took, in order, no matter which department handled it.

**One line to remember:** ELK pools every service's logs into one searchable place, and a correlation ID lets you pull the complete story of a single request out of billions of log lines with one filter.

sections.s2_technical:
In a microservices system, logs are a problem precisely because they are scattered. Each service runs in multiple Pods, each Pod writes logs to its own ephemeral filesystem, and a single customer action may touch five services. Without centralization, diagnosing an issue means logging into many Pods and correlating by hand, and when a Pod is recreated its logs vanish. The ELK stack solves this by shipping all logs into one durable, searchable store.

Elasticsearch is the heart. It is a distributed search engine that stores each log line as a JSON document in an index, building an inverted index so that searching across billions of log lines is fast. Logs are usually written into time-based indices, for example one per day, which makes it easy to retain recent data on fast storage and expire or archive old data.

Logstash or Beats does the collection. In a modern Kubernetes setup, a lightweight shipper such as Filebeat runs as a DaemonSet, meaning one agent per node, tailing the container log files, enriching each line with metadata like the Pod name and namespace, and forwarding to Elasticsearch, sometimes via Logstash for heavier parsing. The key enabler is that the application itself logs in structured JSON rather than plain text, so fields like the service name, log level, timestamp, and correlation ID arrive as queryable fields, not as a blob of text you have to parse later.

Kibana is the window. It connects to Elasticsearch and lets engineers run searches in a query language, build visualisations such as error-rate-over-time charts, and assemble dashboards. In practice you configure Kibana by pointing it at the Elasticsearch cluster, creating an index pattern that tells Kibana which indices to read and which field is the timestamp, and then saving searches and dashboards the team reuses. For an on-call engineer, the typical workflow is to open Kibana's Discover view, filter by the service and a time range, and narrow down to the error.

Correlation IDs are what turn centralized logging into true request tracing. When a request first enters the system, usually at the API gateway or the first service, it is assigned a unique correlation ID, often a UUID, or it reuses one supplied in a request header if the call came from another internal service. That ID is placed into the logging context so every log line written during that request automatically includes it. In a Java application this is done with the Mapped Diagnostic Context, or MDC, which is a per-thread map that the logging framework merges into each log line. Crucially, the service also forwards the correlation ID in the headers of any outbound call to a downstream service, and that service reads the header and puts it into its own MDC, so the same ID flows end to end.

The payoff is dramatic. When Rajesh reports a failed transfer, the engineer finds the correlation ID from the error response or an audit record, types it into Kibana, and sees every log line from the gateway, the transfer service, the fraud service, and the account service for that one request, in time order, across all Pods. What would have been an hour of cross-referencing becomes a ten-second filter.

The senior-level nuance is the relationship between logging and distributed tracing. Correlation IDs in logs give you the thread to pull, but full distributed tracing tools add timing and a parent-child span relationship so you can also see how long each hop took and where the latency was. A mature setup uses a standard like the W3C traceparent header so the trace ID and the log correlation ID are the same value, letting you jump from a slow trace in a tracing tool straight to the matching logs in Kibana. Two other production concerns matter: never log sensitive data such as full account numbers or passwords into Elasticsearch, because those logs are broadly searchable, and manage index lifecycle so you retain what compliance requires and expire the rest to control cost.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a transfer from Rajesh to Priya passes through an API gateway, the Transfer Service, the Fraud Service, and the Account Service. Rajesh reports that one transfer failed, and the on-call engineer must find out why.

Problem 1 — The four services each run several Pods, and the logs for Rajesh's request are spread across many Pods on many nodes. Without centralization, the engineer cannot even find all the relevant log lines. This is exactly what the ELK stack solves: every service ships structured JSON logs into one Elasticsearch cluster that Kibana can search.

Problem 2 — Even with all logs in one place, there are millions of lines. The engineer needs to isolate just the lines belonging to Rajesh's one failed transfer. This is exactly what a correlation ID solves: the gateway stamped the request with a unique ID that every service attached to every log line, so one filter in Kibana isolates the whole request.

Problem 3 — The correlation ID must travel across service boundaries, not just within one service. If the Transfer Service calls the Fraud Service without passing the ID, the fraud logs would be orphaned. This is exactly what header propagation plus the Mapped Diagnostic Context solve: the ID rides in an HTTP header and is placed into each service's logging context.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that simulates the request flowing through the services, each producing structured log lines tagged with a shared correlation ID, and an in-memory `LogStore` that stands in for Elasticsearch. A `CorrelationContext` models the MDC. A `KibanaQuery` class then filters the store by correlation ID, reproducing exactly what an engineer does in Kibana's Discover view. The demo runs one successful transfer and one failed transfer, then queries by the failed transfer's correlation ID to show the complete cross-service story.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two transfer requests from Rajesh to Priya, one for fifty thousand rupees that succeeds and one for nine hundred thousand rupees that the fraud service blocks.

Step 1: The first request arrives at the gateway. The gateway mints a correlation ID, places it into the correlation context, and writes a log line tagged with that ID into the store, which represents indexing a document into Elasticsearch.

Step 2: The gateway calls the Transfer Service, explicitly passing the same correlation ID, mirroring how a real service forwards it in an HTTP header. The Transfer Service writes its own log line with the identical ID, so its logs join the same request story.

Step 3: The Transfer Service calls the Fraud Service with the same ID. The amount of fifty thousand is below the threshold, so the Fraud Service logs a normal score and returns not flagged. The Transfer Service then calls the Account Service, again with the same ID, which logs the debit and credit. Finally the Transfer Service logs that the transfer completed. All of these lines carry one correlation ID.

Step 4: The second request repeats the flow with a fresh correlation ID, but the amount of nine hundred thousand exceeds the fraud threshold. The Fraud Service logs a warning and returns flagged, and the Transfer Service logs an error that the transfer was blocked. This second request's lines all carry a different correlation ID from the first.

Step 5: The demo finds the correlation ID of the blocked request by locating the line containing the blocked message. This mirrors how an engineer would get the ID from an error response or audit record.

Step 6: KibanaQuery filters the entire store by that one correlation ID, exactly as an engineer types the filter into Kibana's Discover view. It returns only the lines for the failed request — the gateway receiving it, the transfer service validating, the fraud service flagging, and the transfer service blocking — in order, across all services. The successful request's lines are excluded because they carry a different ID.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The ELK stack is three tools that together solve the scattered-logs problem in a microservices system. Elasticsearch is a distributed search engine that stores each log line as a JSON document and builds an inverted index so searching billions of lines is fast. Logstash or the lighter Beats agents collect logs from every service and ship them in; in a Kubernetes setup I run Filebeat as a DaemonSet, one agent per node, tailing container logs and enriching them with Pod metadata. And Kibana is the web interface where engineers search, visualise, and build dashboards. I configure Kibana by pointing it at the Elasticsearch cluster, creating an index pattern over the daily log indices with the timestamp field, and saving the searches and dashboards the team reuses.

The thing that makes centralized logging genuinely powerful is the correlation ID. When a request first enters the system at the gateway, I assign it a unique ID, or reuse one passed in a header from an upstream internal service, and I put it into the logging context — in Java that is the Mapped Diagnostic Context, a per-thread map the logging framework merges into every log line. So every line written while handling that request automatically carries the ID. Critically, the service also forwards the ID in the headers of any downstream call, and the next service reads it into its own context, so the same ID flows end to end across every service the request touches.

The payoff is what sells it in an interview. When Rajesh reports a failed transfer, I get the correlation ID from the error response or an audit record, type it into Kibana's Discover view as a single filter, and instantly see every log line from the gateway, the transfer service, the fraud service, and the account service for that one request, in time order, across all Pods. What used to be an hour of logging into individual Pods and cross-referencing by hand becomes a ten-second filter that reveals, for example, that the fraud service blocked the transfer because the amount exceeded a threshold.

At National Bank of India I also kept two production disciplines front of mind. First, the correlation ID is tied to our distributed tracing so the trace ID and the log ID are the same value, letting me jump from a slow trace straight to the matching logs. Second, we never logged sensitive data like full account numbers or passwords into Elasticsearch, because those logs are broadly searchable, and we used index lifecycle management to retain what compliance required and expire the rest to control storage cost. So ELK plus correlation IDs did not just make debugging fast; it did so in a way that respected the security and cost realities of a regulated bank.

answers.question: What is Elasticsearch, and how does it search internally (inverted index, analyzers, sharding, near-real-time)?
answers.shortTitle: What Elasticsearch is, and how it searches internally — inverted index, analyzers, sharding, near-real-time

s1_definition.profdef: Elasticsearch is a distributed, document-oriented search and analytics engine built on top of Apache Lucene. It stores data as JSON documents in indices and makes them searchable in near-real-time through four core mechanisms. The inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it, which is what makes full-text search fast. Analyzers transform text into normalized terms during both indexing and querying so that searches match regardless of case, punctuation, or word form. Sharding splits an index into pieces distributed across nodes so data and query load scale horizontally, with replicas providing redundancy. Near-real-time means a newly indexed document becomes searchable after a short refresh interval, typically one second, rather than instantly, because Lucene buffers writes and periodically makes them visible.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the back of a thick banking regulations manual at National Bank of India. Instead of reading every page to find the word "overdraft," you flip to the index at the back, which lists "overdraft" and the exact pages it appears on. That back-of-book index is an inverted index. The analyzer is the librarian who, before building that index, lowercases everything and ignores commas so "Overdraft," and "overdraft" land on the same entry. Sharding is splitting the enormous manual into ten volumes kept in ten different rooms so ten clerks can search at once. And near-real-time is the rule that a newly added page shows up in the index a second after it is filed, not the instant the ink dries.
s1_definition.oneliner: Elasticsearch flips the problem around — instead of scanning documents for a word, it keeps a word-to-documents map, splits it across machines, and refreshes it about once a second.
s1_definition.raw:

It stores data as JSON documents in indices and makes them searchable in near-real-time through four core mechanisms. The inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it, which is what makes full-text search fast. Analyzers transform text into normalized terms during both indexing and querying so that searches match regardless of case, punctuation, or word form. Sharding splits an index into pieces distributed across nodes so data and query load scale horizontally, with replicas providing redundancy. Near-real-time means a newly indexed document becomes searchable after a short refresh interval, typically one second, rather than instantly, because Lucene buffers writes and periodically makes them visible.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the back of a thick banking regulations manual at National Bank of India. Instead of reading every page to find the word "overdraft," you flip to the index at the back, which lists "overdraft" and the exact pages it appears on. That back-of-book index is an inverted index. The analyzer is the librarian who, before building that index, lowercases everything and ignores commas so "Overdraft," and "overdraft" land on the same entry. Sharding is splitting the enormous manual into ten volumes kept in ten different rooms so ten clerks can search at once. And near-real-time is the rule that a newly added page shows up in the index a second after it is filed, not the instant the ink dries.

**One line to remember:** Elasticsearch flips the problem around — instead of scanning documents for a word, it keeps a word-to-documents map, splits it across machines, and refreshes it about once a second.

sections.s2_technical:
Elasticsearch stores data as JSON documents grouped into an index, which is roughly analogous to a table in a relational database but optimized for search rather than transactional updates. Each document has fields, and the mapping describes the type of each field. Under the hood every index is powered by Apache Lucene, and most of the clever search behaviour comes from Lucene; Elasticsearch adds the distributed layer, the REST API, and cluster management on top.

The inverted index is the foundational data structure. A normal, or forward, index would map each document to the words it contains. An inverted index does the reverse: it maps each unique term to the sorted list of documents that contain it, called a postings list, often with the positions of the term within each document. So to find all documents containing "overdraft," Elasticsearch does not scan every document; it looks up "overdraft" once in the term dictionary and reads the postings list. This is why search stays fast even across billions of documents, and it is the same principle as the index at the back of a book.

Analyzers decide what the terms in that inverted index actually are. When a text field is indexed, it passes through an analyzer composed of three stages. Character filters may strip or replace characters, for example removing HTML. A tokenizer breaks the text into tokens, typically splitting on whitespace and punctuation, so "overdraft protection" becomes the tokens "overdraft" and "protection." Token filters then normalize the tokens, commonly lowercasing them, removing stop words like "the," and sometimes stemming so "transferring" and "transferred" reduce to a common root "transfer." The crucial point is that the same analyzer runs at query time, so a user searching for "Transferred" is normalized to the same term that was stored, and the match succeeds. This is why full-text search feels forgiving of case and word form. For fields where you want exact matching, such as a status code or an account ID, you use the keyword type, which is not analyzed and is stored verbatim.

Sharding is how Elasticsearch scales horizontally and stays available. When you create an index you choose a number of primary shards; each shard is itself a complete, independent Lucene index holding a subset of the documents. Elasticsearch decides which shard a document belongs to by hashing its routing value, usually the document id, so documents spread evenly. Because each shard is independent, a search is sent to every shard in parallel, each returns its best matches, and the coordinating node merges them, which is how query throughput scales with the number of nodes. Replica shards are copies of primaries placed on different nodes; they provide fault tolerance, since if a node holding a primary fails a replica is promoted, and they also serve read traffic, increasing search capacity. The number of primary shards is fixed at index creation, which is why sizing shards appropriately up front matters.

Near-real-time search is a direct consequence of how Lucene handles writes. When you index a document it is first written to an in-memory buffer and to a durable transaction log called the translog for crash safety, but it is not yet searchable. Periodically, by default every second, a refresh operation takes the buffered documents and writes them into a new Lucene segment that becomes searchable. So there is a small delay, the refresh interval, between indexing a document and being able to find it. This design is a deliberate trade-off: batching writes into segments is far more efficient than making every single write immediately searchable, and a one-second delay is irrelevant for log search and analytics. Segments are immutable once written; updates and deletes are handled by marking old documents as deleted and writing new segments, and a background merge process periodically combines small segments into larger ones and purges deleted documents.

The senior-level nuance is understanding the trade-offs this architecture implies. Elasticsearch is optimized for read-heavy search and analytics, not for the strong transactional consistency of a relational database; it offers no multi-document transactions and only near-real-time visibility. Choosing the right number of shards matters because too many small shards waste overhead while too few huge shards cannot be rebalanced or parallelized well. The analyzer choice determines search quality, and mismatched index-time and query-time analyzers are a classic cause of "why does my search return nothing." And because the inverted index plus segment model favours append and search over frequent single-document updates, Elasticsearch shines for logs, metrics, product catalogues, and full-text search, while the system of record for money stays in a transactional database.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the fraud and support teams need to search millions of transaction audit records by free text — for example finding every record mentioning "international wire" for a given account — far faster than a relational database scan allows.

Problem 1 — A support agent types "International Wire" but the stored text reads "international wire transfer." A literal, case-sensitive match would find nothing. This is exactly what analyzers solve: both the stored text and the query are lowercased and tokenized, so the terms line up and the match succeeds.

Problem 2 — There are millions of records, and scanning each one for the words is far too slow. This is exactly what the inverted index solves: each term points directly to the records that contain it, so the search reads a short postings list instead of every document.

Problem 3 — The volume is too large for one machine, and the team cannot afford downtime if a node fails. This is exactly what sharding and replicas solve: the index is split across shards for parallel search and copied to replicas for resilience.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that models these internals. It will contain an `Analyzer` that lowercases and tokenizes text, an `InvertedIndex` mapping terms to document ids, a `Shard` that holds its own inverted index for a subset of documents, and a `SearchEngine` that routes documents to shards by hashing, queries all shards in parallel, and merges results. The demo indexes several transaction audit documents, then searches for a phrase to show how analysis plus the inverted index produce fast, forgiving matches across shards.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four transaction audit documents, two mentioning international wire transfers with different casing, indexed into a three-shard engine, then a search for the phrase "International Wire."

Step 1: Document TXN-1 is indexed. The engine hashes its id and takes the result modulo three to pick a shard, then hands the document to that shard. The shard's analyzer turns "International Wire transfer to London" into the terms international, wire, transfer, london, dropping the stop word "to," and adds TXN-1 to each of those terms' postings lists.

Step 2: TXN-2, TXN-3, and TXN-4 are indexed the same way. Routing by hash spreads them across the three shards. Note TXN-3's text "international wire incoming from Dubai" produces the same lowercased terms international and wire as TXN-1, even though TXN-1 used capitals, because the analyzer lowercases both.

Step 3: The search for "International Wire" begins. The query runs through the identical analyzer, producing the terms international and wire. This is the crucial step: because the query is analyzed with the same rules as the documents, the capitalized query terms become the same lowercased terms that were stored.

Step 4: The engine fans the query out to all three shards in parallel. Each shard looks up "international" and "wire" in its own inverted index and intersects the postings lists, returning only documents that contain both terms. Shards holding TXN-1 and TXN-3 return those ids; shards holding TXN-2 and TXN-4 return nothing because those documents lack both terms.

Step 5: The coordinating engine merges the per-shard results into one set. The final answer is TXN-1 and TXN-3 — exactly the two international wire records — found by reading short postings lists rather than scanning every document, and matched despite the difference in capitalization.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 2:30:11 AM com.bank.search.engine.SearchEngine search
INFO: shard 0 matched [TXN-1]
INFO: shard 2 matched [TXN-3]
Oct 25, 2026 2:30:11 AM com.bank.search.SearchDemo main
INFO: query 'International Wire' matched docs = [TXN-1, TXN-3]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Elasticsearch is a distributed, document-oriented search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene. It stores data as JSON documents in indices and makes them searchable in near-real-time. Four internal mechanisms explain how it searches so fast. The first is the inverted index: rather than mapping each document to the words it contains, it maps each unique term to the sorted list of documents that contain it, so finding every record mentioning "overdraft" is a single lookup plus reading a short postings list, not a scan of every document. That is the same idea as the index at the back of a book, and it is why search stays fast across billions of records.

The second mechanism is analyzers, which decide what the terms in that index actually are. When text is indexed it passes through character filters, a tokenizer that splits it into tokens, and token filters that lowercase, remove stop words, and sometimes stem words to a common root. The critical detail is that the very same analyzer runs at query time, so a user searching "International Wire" is normalized to the same lowercased terms that were stored, and the match succeeds despite the difference in casing. For fields that need exact matching, like an account id or a status code, I use the keyword type, which is stored verbatim and not analyzed.

The third mechanism is sharding. An index is split into primary shards, each a complete independent Lucene index holding a subset of the documents, and Elasticsearch routes a document to a shard by hashing its id so data spreads evenly. A search is scattered to every shard in parallel and the results are gathered and merged, which is how query throughput scales with the number of nodes. Replica shards are copies on other nodes that provide fault tolerance and extra read capacity. The fourth mechanism is near-real-time: a newly indexed document is buffered and written to a durable translog, but only becomes searchable after a refresh, by default every second, because batching writes into immutable Lucene segments is far more efficient than making every single write instantly visible.

The judgement I bring to interviews is knowing where this architecture fits and where it does not. Elasticsearch is superb for read-heavy full-text search, logs, metrics, and analytics, but it offers no multi-document transactions and only near-real-time consistency, so at National Bank of India the system of record for money always stayed in a transactional database, while Elasticsearch powered the fraud and support teams' fast searching over millions of transaction audit records. I size shards deliberately because too many tiny shards waste overhead and too few giant ones cannot parallelize, and I keep index-time and query-time analyzers consistent, because a mismatch there is the classic reason a search mysteriously returns nothing.

answers.question: What is the default mapping type in Elasticsearch (`_doc`), and why were multiple types removed?
answers.shortTitle: The default mapping type in Elasticsearch (`_doc`) and why multiple types were removed

s1_definition.profdef: In older Elasticsearch, an index could contain multiple mapping types, which were named sub-groupings of documents within one index, loosely analogous to tables inside a database. Starting in version six, Elasticsearch deprecated multiple types and restricted each index to a single type, and from version seven onward that single type is the fixed, implicit value `_doc`. Multiple types were removed because they were a leaky abstraction: all types in one index shared the same underlying Lucene index, so fields with the same name across different types had to share one definition, which caused mapping conflicts, sparse storage, and confusing behaviour. The single `_doc` type eliminates that whole class of problems, and type-related URL segments and parameters have been progressively removed from the API.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India once kept savings customers and loan customers in the same ledger book but labelled each row as either a "savings" row or a "loan" row. The trouble was that both kinds of rows had to use the exact same column definitions, so if savings used "balance" as money and loans used "balance" as remaining principal with a different format, they clashed, and most rows left most columns blank. The bank eventually said: one ledger book holds exactly one kind of record, and if you need two kinds, keep two books. The single book type is like `_doc` — every record in an index is just "a document," with no competing sub-labels.
s1_definition.oneliner: Multiple types pretended to be separate tables but secretly shared one storage, so Elasticsearch replaced them with a single implicit type, `_doc`, and the rule "one index, one kind of document."

Starting in version six, Elasticsearch deprecated multiple types and restricted each index to a single type, and from version seven onward that single type is the fixed, implicit value `_doc`. Multiple types were removed because they were a leaky abstraction: all types in one index shared the same underlying Lucene index, so fields with the same name across different types had to share one definition, which caused mapping conflicts, sparse storage, and confusing behaviour. **In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India once kept savings customers and loan customers in the same ledger book but labelled each row as either a "savings" row or a "loan" row. The trouble was that both kinds of rows had to use the exact same column definitions, so if savings used "balance" as money and loans used "balance" as remaining principal with a different format, they clashed, and most rows left most columns blank. The bank eventually said: one ledger book holds exactly one kind of record, and if you need two kinds, keep two books. The single book type is like `_doc` — every record in an index is just "a document," with no competing sub-labels.

**One line to remember:** Multiple types pretended to be separate tables but secretly shared one storage, so Elasticsearch replaced them with a single implicit type, `_doc`, and the rule "one index, one kind of document."

sections.s2_technical:
To understand the change you need to know what a mapping type originally was. In Elasticsearch versions before six, you created an index and could define several types within it, for example a "customer" type and a "transaction" type in the same index. Each type had its own mapping describing its fields. People reached for this because it looked like a relational database where one database holds many tables, so they assumed one index could hold many types the same way.

The problem is that this analogy was false under the hood. In a relational database, two tables are genuinely independent: a column named "value" in one table has no relationship to a column named "value" in another. In Elasticsearch, all types within a single index were stored in the same Apache Lucene index. Lucene has no concept of types at all; it only sees fields. So if the "customer" type and the "transaction" type both had a field called "value," they were in fact the same Lucene field and had to share a single definition. If one wanted "value" to be a number and the other wanted it to be text, that was an irreconcilable mapping conflict, and Elasticsearch would reject it.

This shared-field reality caused several concrete problems. There were mapping conflicts, as just described, whenever two types used the same field name with different intended types. There was sparse storage and poor compression, because documents of the customer type left all the transaction-only fields empty and vice versa, so the single underlying index was full of blanks, which hurt both storage efficiency and the quality of certain internal statistics. And there was conceptual confusion, because developers reasoned about types as if they were isolated tables when they were not, leading to surprising behaviour.

Elasticsearch therefore began removing multiple types. In version six, an index was limited to a single type. In version seven, specifying a type in most API calls was deprecated, and the type effectively became a fixed internal value, `_doc`. The name `_doc` was chosen partly because it reads naturally in the document APIs and partly as a neutral placeholder meaning "a document," with no suggestion that you should create meaningful type names. In version eight, type references were removed from the APIs more completely, so you simply address an index and its documents without ever naming a type.

The practical migration guidance that replaced multiple types is straightforward: if you previously used two types in one index to model two kinds of entities, you now use two separate indices, one per entity kind, because separate indices are genuinely independent and each has its own field definitions with no sharing. If instead you have documents that are variations of the same kind and only sometimes differ, you keep them in one index and add a plain field, often called something like "type" or "category," to distinguish them, filtering on that field at query time. The difference is that this is now an ordinary field under your control, not a special structural concept with hidden shared-storage consequences.

The senior-level nuance is that this change reflects a broader principle: an abstraction that does not match its implementation is worse than no abstraction. Mapping types promised relational-style isolation but delivered shared Lucene fields, and that mismatch produced bugs and confusion for years. Removing them simplified the mental model to "an index is a collection of similar documents," which aligns exactly with how Lucene actually works. When you work with any modern Elasticsearch client, you will see the document APIs use the `_doc` endpoint, and you should treat the type as a vestigial constant rather than something to design around.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, an older system tried to store both customer profiles and transaction records in a single Elasticsearch index using two mapping types. After an upgrade, the team must redesign to the modern single-type model.

Problem 1 — The customer type had a field "amount" meaning the customer's credit limit as a plain number, while the transaction type had a field "amount" meaning the money moved, which the team wanted formatted differently. Because both lived in one index, they were the same Lucene field and conflicted. This is exactly the mapping-conflict problem that multiple types caused.

Problem 2 — Customer documents left every transaction-only field blank and transactions left every customer-only field blank, so the single index was mostly empty cells. This is exactly the sparse-storage problem that motivated removing types.

Problem 3 — The team needs the modern design. Two genuinely different entities should live in two separate indices, each with its own clean mapping and no field sharing. This is exactly the replacement pattern for multiple types.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that contrasts the old and new models. It will contain a `MappingRegistry` that simulates how a single shared index forces one definition per field name and detects a conflict, and an `IndexCatalog` representing the modern approach where each index has its own independent mapping under the fixed `_doc` type. The demo first reproduces the old conflict, then shows the modern design with separate customer and transaction indices resolving it cleanly.

Input data: an attempt to define a field named "amount" as a number for a customer type and as text for a transaction type in one legacy shared index, followed by the modern design using two separate indices.

Step 1: The legacy SharedIndex is created. The customer type defines the field "amount" as a long, which represents a credit limit stored as a number. The shared field map now records that "amount" is a long.

Step 2: The transaction type tries to define the same field name "amount" as text, because that type wanted the money value formatted as a string. Because all types in a legacy index share one underlying Lucene field, the code finds that "amount" is already defined as a long and detects an irreconcilable conflict.

Step 3: The conflict throws an exception, and the demo logs the failure with its full message. This reproduces exactly the real-world mapping conflict that multiple types caused: two "types" could never truly have independent definitions for a same-named field.

Step 4: The modern design begins. The IndexCatalog creates a "customers" index. Its single implicit type is `_doc`, and it owns its own field space. The customer index defines "amount" as a long with no interference from anything else.

Step 5: The catalog creates a separate "transactions" index, also with the implicit `_doc` type and its own independent field space. This index defines "amount" as a scaled float suited to money. Because the two indices are genuinely separate, the two definitions of "amount" never touch each other.

Step 6: The catalog describes both indices, showing each with type `_doc` and its own clean "amount" definition. The conflict that was unavoidable in the old model simply cannot occur in the new one, because separation is real rather than pretended.

sections.s6_takeaway:
In older Elasticsearch, an index could contain multiple mapping types, which were named sub-groupings of documents inside one index that people treated like tables inside a database. From version six onward Elasticsearch deprecated multiple types and limited each index to a single type, and from version seven that single type became a fixed implicit value, `_doc`. So in modern Elasticsearch you never create meaningful type names; every document in an index is simply a `_doc`, and the document APIs reflect that with endpoints like slash index slash underscore doc.

The reason multiple types were removed is that they were a leaky abstraction. The relational analogy that one index could hold many independent types the way a database holds many independent tables was false under the hood. All types within one index were stored in the same Apache Lucene index, and Lucene has no concept of types at all — it only sees fields. So if two types both had a field named "amount," they were physically the same Lucene field and had to share one definition. If one wanted it as a number and the other as text, that was an irreconcilable mapping conflict. On top of that, documents of one type left all the other type's fields blank, producing sparse, poorly compressed storage, and the mismatch between the mental model and the reality caused years of confusing bugs.

The modern replacement is simple and I apply it directly. If I previously used two types in one index to model two genuinely different entities, I now use two separate indices, one per entity, because separate indices really are independent and each owns its own field definitions with no sharing. If instead I have documents that are variations of the same kind, I keep them in one index and add an ordinary field, perhaps called "category," to distinguish them and filter on it at query time — but that is now a normal field under my control, not a special structural concept with hidden shared-storage consequences.

At National Bank of India, we hit exactly this when an older system had crammed customer profiles and transaction records into one index using two types, and a field named "amount" meant a credit limit for customers but a money value for transactions, which collided. The fix was to split them into a customers index and a transactions index, each with the implicit `_doc` type and its own clean mapping, so "amount" could be a plain long in one and a scaled float in the other with no conflict. The broader lesson I take from it is that an abstraction which does not match its implementation is worse than no abstraction, and removing mapping types gave Elasticsearch a mental model — an index is a collection of similar documents — that finally matches how Lucene actually works.

answers.question: Is the default string field type in Elasticsearch `text` or `keyword`, and how does dynamic mapping handle it?
answers.shortTitle: The default string field type in Elasticsearch — `text` or `keyword` — and how dynamic mapping handles it

s1_definition.profdef: When Elasticsearch encounters a string field it has never seen and you have not defined a mapping for it, dynamic mapping automatically maps it as a multi-field: the field itself is typed as `text`, which is analyzed for full-text search, and a sub-field named `keyword` is added, typed as `keyword`, which is stored verbatim for exact matching, sorting, and aggregations. So the honest answer is that neither is "the" single default — the default is both at once, with `text` as the main field and `keyword` as a sub-field (by default capped at 256 characters). The `text` type tokenizes and lowercases the value so you can search for words inside it, while the `keyword` type keeps the whole string unbroken so you can filter, sort, and group on the exact value.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India files a customer's full address. The bank keeps it in two forms. One form is chopped into searchable words — "street," "mumbai," "india" — so a clerk can find anyone living in Mumbai; that is the `text` form. The other form is the whole address kept exactly as written on one line, used when you need to match the precise address or group customers by it; that is the `keyword` form. When the bank first sees a new kind of field, it automatically files it in both forms, just in case you need to search inside it and also match it exactly.
s1_definition.oneliner: A new string field is dynamically mapped as `text` for searching words inside it, with a `.keyword` sub-field for exact match, sort, and aggregation — you get both unless you declare otherwise.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When Elasticsearch encounters a string field it has never seen and you have not defined a mapping for it, dynamic mapping automatically maps it as a multi-field: the field itself is typed as `text`, which is analyzed for full-text search, and a sub-field named `keyword` is added, typed as `keyword`, which is stored verbatim for exact matching, sorting, and aggregations. So the honest answer is that neither is "the" single default — the default is both at once, with `text` as the main field and `keyword` as a sub-field (by default capped at 256 characters). The `text` type tokenizes and lowercases the value so you can search for words inside it, while the `keyword` type keeps the whole string unbroken so you can filter, sort, and group on the exact value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India files a customer's full address. The bank keeps it in two forms. One form is chopped into searchable words — "street," "mumbai," "india" — so a clerk can find anyone living in Mumbai; that is the `text` form. The other form is the whole address kept exactly as written on one line, used when you need to match the precise address or group customers by it; that is the `keyword` form. When the bank first sees a new kind of field, it automatically files it in both forms, just in case you need to search inside it and also match it exactly.

**One line to remember:** A new string field is dynamically mapped as `text` for searching words inside it, with a `.keyword` sub-field for exact match, sort, and aggregation — you get both unless you declare otherwise.

sections.s2_technical:
To answer precisely you have to separate two things: what type a string becomes, and how dynamic mapping decides that. Dynamic mapping is the behaviour where, if you index a document containing a field that is not in the index's mapping, Elasticsearch infers a type from the value and adds it to the mapping automatically. For a JSON string value, the inferred result since version five is not a single type but a multi-field. The top-level field is mapped as `text`, and underneath it Elasticsearch adds a sub-field called `keyword` mapped as the `keyword` type, with an `ignore_above` setting of 256 so that strings longer than 256 characters are not indexed as a keyword, protecting against giant values bloating the index.

The `text` type is for full-text search. When a value is indexed into a text field it passes through an analyzer that tokenizes and normalizes it, so "International Wire Transfer" becomes the terms international, wire, and transfer. This lets a match query find the document when the user searches for any of those words regardless of case. But because the original value was broken into tokens, a text field by default cannot be used efficiently for sorting or for aggregations that group by the exact original value, and it does not support exact-equality filtering on the whole string.

The `keyword` type is the opposite. The value is stored as a single, exact, un-analyzed term. "International Wire Transfer" stays as that whole string. This is what you use for structured identifiers and categorical data: an account id, a status like SETTLED or FAILED, a currency code, a country. Keyword fields support exact-term filtering, sorting, and aggregations such as counting how many transactions are in each status, because grouping needs the whole unbroken value.

The reason dynamic mapping gives you both is that at the moment a new field first appears, Elasticsearch does not know your intent. You might want to search inside the text, or you might want to filter and aggregate on the exact value, or both. By creating the `text` field plus the `keyword` sub-field, it hedges: you reach the searchable form by the field name itself, and the exact form by appending dot keyword, for example querying the field for a match but aggregating on field dot keyword.

There is important nuance about which fields get this treatment. Dynamic mapping infers other JSON types too: a JSON number becomes a numeric type like long or float, a boolean becomes boolean, and a string that looks like a date can be mapped as a date if date detection is enabled, which is why a field containing "2026-10-25" might unexpectedly become a date rather than text. This date detection surprising people is a common gotcha. Dynamic mapping also has modes you can set per index: the default true adds new fields automatically, runtime adds them as runtime fields evaluated at query time, false ignores unknown fields but still stores them, and strict rejects documents containing unmapped fields, which is the safest choice for a production index where you want full control.

The senior-level guidance is that relying on dynamic mapping for a production index is convenient but risky, so experienced teams usually define explicit mappings. If every string automatically becomes text-plus-keyword, you can double your index size storing two representations of fields you only ever filter on, and you can get the wrong type when date detection misfires. For a banking audit index I would explicitly map an account id and a status as pure `keyword`, a free-text description as `text`, and a timestamp as a `date`, and I would often set dynamic to strict so an unexpected field in a document is rejected rather than silently and perhaps wrongly mapped. Dynamic mapping is excellent for exploration and for log data whose shape varies, but for a stable, performance-sensitive schema, explicit mapping is the professional default.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the team indexes transaction records with a free-text description, a status, and an account id. They first let dynamic mapping infer the types, then discover why explicit mapping is better.

Problem 1 — A support agent needs to search descriptions for the word "wire" and find every matching transaction. If the description were stored only as an exact keyword, searching for a single word inside it would fail. This is exactly why the description should be `text`: it is tokenized so word searches work.

Problem 2 — A dashboard needs to count transactions grouped by status, such as how many are SETTLED versus FAILED. If status were only `text`, it would be broken into tokens and could not be grouped by its exact value. This is exactly why status should be `keyword`: the whole value is kept for aggregation.

Problem 3 — Letting dynamic mapping map everything as text-plus-keyword wastes space on fields like the account id that are only ever filtered exactly, and risks mis-typing. This is exactly why the team moves to an explicit, strict mapping for the production index.

To make this runnable without a real cluster, we will build a small program that models the two field behaviours. It will contain a `TextField` that analyzes values into tokens and supports word-level match, a `KeywordField` that stores values verbatim and supports exact match and grouping, a `DynamicMapper` that, for a new string field, creates a text field with a keyword sub-field, and an `ExplicitMapping` that lets you declare the right type per field. The demo indexes transactions both ways, runs a word search on the description, aggregates by status, and shows why explicit mapping is the production choice.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three transactions, two describing international wire transfers with different casing, with statuses SETTLED, SETTLED, and FAILED.

Step 1: The DynamicMapper is asked about a new string field "description." It records "description" as text and adds "description.keyword" as a keyword with the 256-character cap, exactly reproducing how Elasticsearch dynamically maps a fresh string field into a multi-field.

Step 2: The text field indexes each description. "International Wire transfer" is lowercased and split into the tokens international, wire, transfer. The other two descriptions are tokenized the same way, so TXN-3's "international wire incoming" yields international, wire, incoming.

Step 3: A word search for "wire" runs against the text field. It lowercases the query and finds every document whose token set contains "wire," returning TXN-1 and TXN-3. This works precisely because text fields are analyzed into words; searching inside the string is possible.

Step 4: The keyword field indexes each status verbatim: SETTLED, SETTLED, FAILED, with no tokenization. An exact term query for "FAILED" returns only TXN-3, matching the whole unbroken value.

Step 5: A terms aggregation groups by exact status value and counts each group, producing SETTLED mapped to two and FAILED mapped to one. This works precisely because keyword fields keep the whole value, which is what grouping requires; a text field could not do this correctly because it would have split the values into tokens.

Step 6: The explicit production mapping is defined, assigning description to text, status and account id to keyword, and created_at to date — each field exactly the type it needs with no wasted dual representation. Finally the demo tries to index a field that is not in the mapping, and because the mapping is strict, that field is rejected, demonstrating the safety of controlling the schema rather than letting dynamic mapping guess.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The precise answer is that neither `text` nor `keyword` alone is the default for a string in Elasticsearch — the default produced by dynamic mapping is both at once. When Elasticsearch meets a string field it has not seen and you have not defined, dynamic mapping creates a multi-field: the top-level field is mapped as `text`, which is analyzed for full-text search, and under it a sub-field named `keyword` is added, mapped as the `keyword` type with an ignore-above setting of 256 so overly long strings are not indexed as a keyword. So out of the box you can both search for words inside the value using the field name and match, sort, or aggregate on the exact value using the field name followed by dot keyword.

The two types exist because they do opposite jobs. A `text` field is analyzed — tokenized and lowercased — so "International Wire transfer" becomes the terms international, wire, and transfer, which is what lets a match query find the document when a user searches for any of those words regardless of case. But because the value was broken into tokens, a text field cannot by default be used for exact-equality filtering, sorting, or aggregating on the whole original value. A `keyword` field is the reverse: the whole value is stored verbatim and un-analyzed, which is exactly what you need for identifiers and categorical data like an account id, a status such as SETTLED or FAILED, or a currency code, because exact filtering and grouping require the unbroken value.

Dynamic mapping hedges by giving you both because, at the instant a new field first appears, Elasticsearch does not know your intent. It also infers other types — numbers become numeric, booleans become boolean, and a string that looks like a date can be mapped as a date if date detection is on, which is a common and surprising gotcha. And it has modes: the default true adds new fields automatically, false stores but ignores them, and strict rejects documents with unmapped fields entirely.

In production I treat dynamic mapping as convenient for exploration and for variable-shaped log data, but I define explicit mappings for stable, performance-sensitive indices. At National Bank of India, for the transactions audit index I explicitly mapped the description as `text` so support could search words inside it, the status and account id as `keyword` so dashboards could aggregate and compliance could filter exactly, and the timestamp as a `date`. I usually set dynamic to strict as well, so an unexpected field in a document is rejected rather than silently and perhaps wrongly mapped — for example a date-looking string sneaking in as a date. Relying on the automatic text-plus-keyword default everywhere would have doubled the index size storing two representations of fields I only ever filtered on, so controlling the schema explicitly was the professional choice.

answers.question: What is Liquibase, and how does it manage database schema version control (changeSets, changelogs, databasechangelog)?
answers.shortTitle: What Liquibase is and how it manages database schema version control — changeSets, changelogs, databasechangelog

s1_definition.profdef: Liquibase is an open-source database schema change-management tool that brings version control to the database the same way git brings it to code. You describe every schema change as a changeSet — a uniquely identified, ordered unit of change such as creating a table or adding a column — and you organize changeSets into a changelog file that Liquibase reads in order. When Liquibase runs against a database, it records every applied changeSet in a tracking table called DATABASECHANGELOG, so on the next run it knows exactly which changeSets are already applied and executes only the new ones. This makes schema evolution repeatable, ordered, and identical across every environment, and it supports rollback and safe team collaboration.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a master ledger of every structural change ever made to its record-keeping system: "added a column for UPI reference on this date," "created the loans table on that date." Each entry is numbered and signed, and the bank keeps a checklist of which changes each branch has already carried out. When a new branch opens, staff simply run down the master list in order, skipping anything already done, so every branch ends up with exactly the same structure. Liquibase is that master ledger and checklist for the database schema, and DATABASECHANGELOG is the checklist of what each database has already applied.
s1_definition.oneliner: Liquibase is git for your database schema — ordered changeSets in a changelog, and a DATABASECHANGELOG table that remembers what has already been applied so each environment converges to the same structure safely.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem Liquibase solves is that databases drift. Without a tool, one developer runs a CREATE TABLE by hand on their machine, another forgets to apply it to staging, and production ends up subtly different, which in a bank is a serious risk. Application code is versioned in git, but the schema it depends on often is not, so the two fall out of sync. Liquibase makes the schema a versioned, reproducible artifact that travels with the code.

A changeSet is the atomic unit. Each changeSet has three identifying parts: an id, an author, and the file it lives in, and together these form a unique identity. A changeSet contains one logical change, such as creating a table, adding a column, creating an index, or inserting seed data. The golden rule is that a changeSet, once committed and applied anywhere, is immutable — you never edit it afterwards, because other databases have already applied it and editing it would make their recorded state inconsistent. If you need to change something, you add a new changeSet. Liquibase enforces this by storing a checksum of each changeSet; if you alter an already-applied changeSet, the checksum no longer matches and Liquibase refuses to run, warning you of the tampering.

A changelog is the ordered master file that lists changeSets, or includes other changelog files. It can be written in SQL, XML, YAML, or JSON. A common structure is a root changelog that includes one file per release or per feature, so the history reads as a clear, append-only timeline. Because the order is explicit and fixed, running the changelog against an empty database reproduces the exact schema step by step, and running it against an existing database applies only what is missing.

The DATABASECHANGELOG table is how Liquibase tracks state inside the database itself. The first time Liquibase runs, it creates this table automatically. For every changeSet it applies, it inserts a row recording the id, author, filename, the checksum, the execution date, and the order. On subsequent runs, Liquibase reads this table, compares it to the changelog, and executes only changeSets that are not already recorded. This is what makes runs idempotent: you can run the same changelog a hundred times and it will only ever apply each changeSet once. There is a companion table, DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK, which holds a lock so that two application instances starting at the same time do not try to apply migrations simultaneously; one acquires the lock and the other waits.

The typical workflow in a banking microservice is that Liquibase runs automatically at application startup or as a dedicated pipeline step before deployment. The developer adds a new changeSet to the changelog, commits it with the code, and when the service starts in any environment, Liquibase brings that environment's schema up to date by applying exactly the new changeSets. Because the same changelog runs everywhere, development, staging, and production schemas stay identical. Liquibase also supports rollback: a changeSet can declare how to undo itself, or Liquibase can auto-generate rollback for simple changes, so you can revert the last few changeSets if a release goes wrong.

The senior-level nuance connects back to safe deployments. For zero-downtime rolling updates where the old and new application versions run simultaneously, schema changes must be backward compatible during the overlap, which is the expand-and-contract pattern, and Liquibase is the tool that executes each of those steps as separate, ordered changeSets: one release adds the new column, a later release removes the old one. You also use preconditions to make changeSets defensive — for example only add a column if it does not already exist — and you use contexts and labels to run certain changeSets only in certain environments, such as inserting test seed data only in development. And critically, destructive changeSets like dropping a column are reviewed carefully and separated from the release that stops using that column, because in a bank you never drop data that a rollback might still need.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, the accounts service needs its schema to evolve safely across many environments and many developers without drift.

Problem 1 — The accounts table must be created once, consistently, everywhere. If each environment were set up by hand, they would diverge. This is exactly what a changeSet in a changelog solves: the create-table change is applied in the same order everywhere.

Problem 2 — Later, a new column for a UPI handle must be added, but only to environments that do not already have it, and without re-running the original create. This is exactly what DATABASECHANGELOG tracking solves: Liquibase applies only the new changeSet because the create-table changeSet is already recorded.

Problem 3 — Two application instances start at once during a rolling deploy and both try to migrate. This is exactly what the DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK solves: only one instance migrates while the other waits.

To make this runnable without a real database, we will build a small program that models Liquibase's engine. It will contain a `ChangeSet` with id, author, forward SQL, and a checksum, a `ChangeLog` holding an ordered list, a `DatabaseChangeLogTable` recording applied changeSets, a `ChangeLogLock` modelling the lock, and a `LiquibaseRunner` that applies only unapplied changeSets and verifies checksums. The demo runs the changelog once to create the table, adds a new changeSet for the UPI column, runs again to show only the new one applies, and attempts to tamper with an applied changeSet to show checksum protection.

```
│   │   └── resources/

│   └── test/
│       └── java/com/bank/liquibase/

│               └── LiquibaseRunnerTest.java
```

The real changelog is part of the deliverable:

```yaml
# src/main/resources/db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml
databaseChangeLog:
  - changeSet:
      id: 1-create-accounts
      author: rajesh
      changes:
        - createTable:
            tableName: accounts
            columns:
              - column: { name: id, type: VARCHAR(20), constraints: { primaryKey: true } }
              - column: { name: holder_name, type: VARCHAR(100) }
              - column: { name: balance, type: DECIMAL(15,2) }
      rollback:
        - dropTable: { tableName: accounts }
  - changeSet:
      id: 2-add-upi-handle
      author: priya
      preConditions:
        - onFail: MARK_RAN
        - not: [ columnExists: { tableName: accounts, columnName: upi_handle } ]
      changes:
        - addColumn:
            tableName: accounts
            columns:
              - column: { name: upi_handle, type: VARCHAR(50) }
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the model
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/accounts-service-1.0.0.jar

# Real Liquibase commands against a database
liquibase --changeLogFile=db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml update
liquibase --changeLogFile=db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml rollbackCount 1
liquibase status   # shows which changeSets are not yet applied
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a changelog starting with one changeSet that creates the accounts table, later gaining a second changeSet that adds a UPI handle column, run against a tracking table that starts empty.

Step 1: On the first run, the runner acquires the changelog lock so no other instance can migrate concurrently. It then reads the changelog, which contains only the create-accounts changeSet.

Step 2: The runner checks the DATABASECHANGELOG tracking table and finds the create-accounts changeSet is not recorded. It applies the forward SQL that creates the table, then records the changeSet's identity and checksum in the tracking table. The lock is released.

Step 3: A second changeSet, add-upi-handle, is appended to the changelog, and the runner is invoked again. It re-acquires the lock and reads both changeSets in order.

Step 4: For the create-accounts changeSet, the runner finds it already recorded in the tracking table and verifies that its stored checksum matches the current one, confirming nobody edited it. Because it is already applied and unchanged, the runner skips it. This is the idempotency that prevents re-creating the table.

Step 5: For the add-upi-handle changeSet, the runner finds it is not yet recorded, so it applies the alter-table forward SQL and records it. Only the new change ran; the environment converged to the latest schema without touching what was already there.

Step 6: To demonstrate protection, the create-accounts changeSet is illegally edited after having been applied. On the next run, the runner computes its checksum, compares it to the stored one, and finds they differ. It throws a checksum-mismatch error and refuses to proceed, exactly as real Liquibase does, because an altered applied changeSet means some databases have a different version of that change and the history is no longer trustworthy.

Final output:

```text
Oct 25, 2026 3:20:14 AM com.bank.liquibase.LiquibaseDemo main
INFO: === first run (fresh database) ===
INFO: applying: 1-create-accounts::rajesh::master.yaml -> CREATE TABLE accounts (id VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(15,2))
INFO: === second run (cs1 already applied) ===
INFO: applying: 2-add-upi-handle::priya::master.yaml -> ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN upi_handle VARCHAR(50)
INFO: === tampering with an applied changeSet ===
SEVERE: Liquibase refused to run: checksum mismatch for 1-create-accounts::rajesh::master.yaml — changeSet was altered!
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  App starts (any environment) → LiquibaseRunner.update(changeLog)
    │
    ▼ acquire DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK (one instance migrates, others wait)
    │
    ▼ read changelog (ordered changeSets)
    │
    ├─ changeSet "1-create-accounts"
    │     in DATABASECHANGELOG?  ── no ──→ apply SQL → record (id, checksum)
    │                            ── yes ─→ checksum match? ── yes → skip
    │                                                      └─ no  → ABORT (tampered)
    │
    ├─ changeSet "2-add-upi-handle"
    │     not recorded ──→ apply ALTER TABLE → record
    │
    ▼ release lock
  Result: every environment converges to the same schema, each change applied once
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Liquibase Engine ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Command/Ledger: each ChangeSet is an applied, recorded command    │
  │     WHY: idempotent re-runs via DATABASECHANGELOG tracking         │
  │  Guarded section: ChangeLogLock serializes concurrent migrations   │
  │     WHY: two instances must not migrate at once                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: ChangeSet=one change, ChangeLog=ordering, Runner=application   │
  │  O: new change = new changeSet; never edit an applied one          │
  │  D: Runner depends on tracking + lock abstractions                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   LiquibaseRunner     │───────▶│  DatabaseChangeLogTable  │
  │ - tracking            │ reads/ │  + isApplied(id)         │
  │ - lock                │ writes │  + storedChecksum(id)    │
  │ + update(changeLog)   │        │  + record(id, checksum)  │
  └──────────┬───────────┘        └──────────────────────────┘
             │ uses                ┌──────────────────────────┐
             ├───────────────────▶ │  ChangeLogLock           │
             │                     │  + acquire() + release() │
             │ iterates            └──────────────────────────┘
             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐◆──────▶┌──────────────────────────┐
  │   ChangeLog           │ owns   │  ChangeSet               │
  │ - changeSets: List    │ (1..*) │  + identity()            │
  │ + add(cs)             │        │  + checksum()            │
  └──────────────────────┘        │  + forwardSql/rollbackSql│
                                   └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: changeSet lifecycle ─────────────────────
  [authored] → [committed to changelog] → [applied + recorded] → [immutable]
        (edit after applied → checksum mismatch → run ABORTS)

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────
  1. LiquibaseRunner.update(changeLog)
  2.   → ChangeLogLock.acquire()
  3.   → for each ChangeSet: tracking.isApplied(identity)?
  4.       → no → apply forwardSql → tracking.record(id, checksum)
  5.       → yes → checksum match? skip : ABORT
  6.   → ChangeLogLock.release()
```

answers.question: What is AGILE and what is SDLC, and how do they differ?
answers.shortTitle: What AGILE and SDLC are, and how they differ

s1_definition.profdef: SDLC, the Software Development Life Cycle, is the overall framework of phases a software product passes through from conception to retirement — typically requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. It describes what work must happen, not how often or in what cadence. Agile is a set of values and principles, defined by the Agile Manifesto, for how to run that life cycle: iteratively and incrementally, in short cycles that deliver working software frequently, welcome changing requirements, and favour close collaboration and feedback over heavy up-front planning. The key distinction is that SDLC is the what — the phases — while Agile is a how — one philosophy of sequencing and executing those phases, in contrast to alternatives like the Waterfall model which runs the same phases once, sequentially, start to finish.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of building National Bank of India's new mobile app. SDLC is the list of stages any construction must go through: figure out what to build, design it, build it, test it, open it to customers, and maintain it. Agile and Waterfall are two different ways to march through those stages. Waterfall is like constructing the entire building in one long sequence — finish all the planning, then all the building, then hand over the keys once at the end. Agile is like building and opening one floor at a time, getting customers to use each floor and give feedback before you build the next, so you can change the design as you learn.
s1_definition.oneliner: SDLC is the set of phases every project goes through; Agile is a way of moving through those phases in short, feedback-driven iterations rather than one big sequential pass.

It describes what work must happen, not how often or in what cadence.
